trajectory_rationale: F1 already announced a customer-centric wallet-share/customer-spend strategy; later filings do not add a stronger qualifying customer-economic mechanism and F5 is dominated by COVID demand/pricing disruption.
Higher full-price ASP, lower discounting and direct-channel mix are explicit at F1 and remain the same established yield mechanism through F5.
Commodity/tariff acquisition-cost increases are explicitly passed through in higher retail/wholesale prices at F1 and repeated through F5.
Filings identify wage/labor and demand risk but no qualifying customer pricing, entitlement, migration or cost-transfer mechanism.

F1 describes tariff/commodity pressure; F2 newly makes customer pass-through, delayed cost recovery and material pass-through clauses explicit. Later filings retain the cost-recovery architecture though F5 is less explicit.
Menu price increases are already an operating sales driver at F1; later filings do not introduce a materially new or stronger customer-yield mechanism.
Commodity-cost escalation clauses and customer/supplier mitigation are explicit at F1 and repeated through F5; no semantic acceleration.
Menu-price actions and their margin/average-check effects are already explicit at F1; later inflation-offset language makes the cost link clearer but does not create a new mechanism.
Filings repeatedly frame possible price increases as a response to product/input costs, but the language remains hypothetical/risk-oriented rather than a concrete customer-transfer action.
Tariffs and freight/raw-material pressure are explicit, but the frozen filings do not establish a concrete company customer-transfer mechanism.
Commodity/tariff and restructuring language does not establish a qualifying customer-economic mechanism.
Tariff effects and potential pass-throughs are discussed, but customer transfer remains uncertain/hypothetical rather than an implemented mechanism.
The 10-K says increased operating costs may not be passable to customers/franchisees; later filings do not convert that risk into a concrete transfer action.
Labor/inflation risks and possible revenue offsets are generic; no qualifying customer-economic action is specified.
Trajectory moves from no qualifying mechanism to a concrete Victoria's Secret profit plan emphasizing full-price selling and then lower promotional activity/more profitable selling at F5.
Inflation risk notes that selling prices may need to rise, but the filings do not establish an implemented or increasingly explicit customer-transfer mechanism.
Tariff-related consumer price transfer is discussed as a limitation/hypothetical; the trajectory does not become a concrete sustained customer action.
Casino/resort filings contain demand and market-risk discussion but no qualifying customer pricing, yield, entitlement, migration or cost-transfer mechanism.
F5 newly makes favorable pricing actions a repeated, explicit driver of gross-margin improvement; this is materially more concrete than the earlier frozen filings.
F2 newly states that industry price increases are generally passed through the supply chain; later filings retain inflation-driven selling-price effects, though F5 wording is less explicit.
The filings discuss an inability to pass certain foreign-currency price increases to customers; this remains a risk statement, not a concrete transfer mechanism.
Tariffs, freight and supply-chain costs are present but no qualifying customer cost-transfer or yield action is identified.
Tariff pressure and inventory rationalization are operational issues without a qualifying customer-economic mechanism.
F1 already states the company is taking pricing actions to mitigate tariff exposure; later filings become less rather than more explicit, so no acceleration is present.
Portfolio divestitures/discontinued operations do not establish customer migration under SP003, and cost inflation language does not become a customer-transfer action.
Tariff and labor/freight pressures are described, but no concrete customer-economic transfer or yield mechanism is identified.
